summary: Flame in Freefall is a searchable web platform for researchers and spacecraft designers that consolidates NASA’s public microgravity combustion data—covering 24 investigations, 277 technical reports, and 138 projects—with one-click source citations. The platform organizes its tools into two core environments: (1) Research Space, featuring a verifiable Research Assistant across 13 switchable AI models with exact document, page, and DOI citations; Investigations and side-by-side Compare profiles; a Discover engine and semantic Evidence Library; and a personal Notebook. (2) Simulation Laboratory, featuring a Flame Simulator that predicts fuel droplet behavior against 257 real FLEX trials, and a 3D Laboratory visualizing complete tests inside FLEX hardware, including invisible "cool flames." Before crews return to the Moon, researchers, mission planners, and safety engineers can determine within minutes what is known about fire in microgravity, what sources of information are available, and what is still unknown, so that the next big leap will be safer.
details:
What it is

Flame in Freefall brings together NASA’s public knowledge on fire in microgravity—24 experimental investigations, 277 technical reports, and 138 research projects—into a single website and makes it searchable in minutes, with the source of every data point just one click away. It is designed for those who research combustion as well as for those who design the next spacecraft or habitat.

What you can do with it

Eleven tools organized into three environments, which are three sections of the application.

Research Space

(1) Research Assistant: the conversational assistant responds by indicating, for every claim, the document, page, and DOI (the permanent code that identifies each scientific publication) from which it originates, and separates what directly answers your question from what is merely related to or expands upon it; it allows switching in real time among 13 language models (via NVIDIA API and Amazon Bedrock) under the same strict verification contract and never presents unrelated external material as if it were an answer. (2) Investigations: the profile of each investigation—its objectives, its experiments, and its publications. (3) Compare: side-by-side comparisons between trials and investigations, two head-to-head with their similarities and differences highlighted. (4) Discover: suggestions of related topics to broaden the search. (5) Evidence: the evidence library—you enter a phrase (e.g., “methanol extinction with CO₂”) and it returns the exact excerpts from NASA documents where it is discussed, each with its source. (6) Notebook: a notebook to save what you have found.

Simulation Laboratory

(7) Flame Simulator: predicts what happens to a fuel droplet based on the pressure, oxygen, and gases you choose; it compares your conditions against the 257 real FLEX trials and relies on the most similar ones, which are displayed in a table. (8) 3D Laboratory: represents the complete test inside the FLEX hardware, including the cool flame that FLEX discovered in orbit (a flame invisible to the naked eye that continues consuming fuel); it also lets you load any real FLEX trial directly into the 3D chamber to compare the actual experimental outcome against the model's prediction.

Mission Data

(9) Mission Dashboard, the application's home view: an overview with the atmosphere and gravity of the ISS (the International Space Station), the Moon, and Mars, with findings calculated from the data—for example, with more than 30% CO₂, 97% of methanol droplets extinguished, and CO₂ happens to be the extinguishing agent used aboard the Station. (10) FLEX Charts: charts of the FLEX trials (the NASA experiment that burned fuel droplets aboard the Station between 2009 and 2011) showing the burning rate—how fast the droplet is consumed—versus available oxygen, extinction probability, and a coverage map that highlights at a glance the combinations of conditions no one has tested in the data. (11) Test Records: each experimental test cataloged with its conditions, its outcome, and a direct link to the original table from which each value was obtained.

How it works

We downloaded and unified the data: 4.2 GB selected from PSI (NASA's physical sciences experiment repository), plus NTRS (its technical reports server) and the Task Book (the catalog of projects funded by NASA). Raw videos and images are not downloaded or indexed (due to time and scope limitations): they remain cataloged in the manifests of each investigation. The 20 experimental tables, each with its own format, are normalized to common units (atm, kelvin, mole fractions) and integrated into a single dataset—each data point preserves its source file and row—, and the result is indexed: 286 documents and over 6,000 searchable passages. Before being displayed, every statement from the assistant is automatically cross-checked against the text of its source using natural language inference (NLI) verification.

RAG Architecture

This diagram illustrates how Flame in Freefall organizes NASA combustion research into an interconnected scientific knowledge network. Instead of treating experimental data, reports, and findings as isolated information, the system establishes meaningful relationships that allow artificial intelligence to understand scientific context, identify relevant evidence, and support reliable comparisons across investigations.

The upper section represents two essential knowledge areas. Combustion Phenomena classifies seven important aspects of flame behavior, including ignition, flame growth, flame spread, stable burning, quenching, blowoff, and extinction. These distinctions help the system recognize that experiments may investigate different combustion processes, particularly under microgravity conditions. Safety Knowledge organizes requirements, NASA standards, design and test criteria, guidance, documented safety implications, and NASA identified research questions. This structure helps distinguish scientific findings from formal safety requirements and prevents unsupported interpretations from being presented as official NASA conclusions.

At the center of the network is Investigation, which connects four major areas of scientific information. Experimental and Property Knowledge organizes experimental runs, materials, samples, measurements, and conditions such as gravity, atmospheric composition, pressure, and flow. Reporting and Source Records preserves the connections between scientific information, original documents, experimental sessions, reported values, and terminology definitions. Instrumentation and Observation identifies equipment, methods, and observations associated with research. Research and Outcomes connects investigations with their objectives, hypotheses, campaigns, documented findings, and scientific conclusions.

The colored connections distinguish different groups of relationships, making the network easier to explore. The underlying ontology defines the scientific concepts, while the Knowledge Graph provides relationships supported by actual research records. Together, these components allow the engine to search beyond simple keyword matching while preserving experimental context and the traceability of scientific information.

The value of this architecture lies in its ability to connect knowledge without losing scientific meaning. Flame in Freefall can identify relationships between investigations, distinguish differences in experimental conditions, retrieve supporting evidence, and help users understand how documented combustion research contributes to spacecraft fire safety. This transforms fragmented NASA research into a structured and explainable foundation for scientific exploration and future human space missions.

Simulator Architecture

1 · The visitor sets the conditions. It all starts with a person who configures the experiment: fuel, oxygen, pressure, gases, and gravity. Every change is posted to an “experiment status,” a shared log that all screens are subscribed to; that’s why the 2D view and the 3D lab never show different things.

2 · The results are based on real NASA data. When a condition is changed, the simulation engine retrieves the current scenario and consults the predictive model, which searches among the 257 real FLEX experiments (the experiment NASA conducted aboard the International Space Station) for the seven most similar to those conditions. This provides estimates of how quickly the droplet burns, whether it goes out, and whether a cold flame appears (the invisible flame that FLEX discovered in orbit, which continues to burn the fuel unseen). And if no one has measured anything similar, the simulator estimates it—by “extrapolating”—rather than inventing a number.

3 · The 3D lab allows you to simulate the experiment. The viewer receives the scene and renders it using Three.js on WebGL 2 (the browser’s 3D graphics standard): the CIR + MDCA combustion chamber, the droplet, the volumetric flame, and the points of interest described in the lab’s script. If the browser does not support WebGL 2, the same model automatically falls back to the 2D canvas renderer.

Cloud architecture (AWS)

The platform is deployed on AWS (us-east-1) with a hybrid architecture that separates in-memory retrieval from compute-intensive neural verification:

  • Domain, DNS, and HTTPS (Amazon Route 53 + Caddy) — the domain flameinfreefall.com resolves in Route 53 to a static Elastic IP, with Caddy acting as a reverse proxy serving static assets and managing automatic TLS certificates (HTTP/2 and HTTP/3).
  • Search and orchestration core (Amazon EC2 Graviton2) — a t4g.large instance (ARM64, Ubuntu 24.04 LTS with a gp3 volume) holds the ontology graph, SQLite database, and semantic vectors in memory, operating two independent lanes (read and conversation) so that querying tables, charts, and records never stalls while the assistant processes a question.
  • Parallel serverless NLI verification (AWS Lambda + Amazon ECR) — the textual entailment verifier (mDeBERTa-v3 on ONNX Runtime) is packaged as an ARM64 container in Amazon ECR and runs on AWS Lambda (flame-nli-verifier). When validating a response, EC2 sends batches of premises and hypotheses in parallel to Lambda—saving over 2 GB of RAM on the primary server—with exact mathematical parity and automatic local fallback in case of contingency.
  • Security and infrastructure (AWS IAM + Amazon S3) — the 1.27 GB of SHA-256-verified runtime assets are backed up in a private Amazon S3 bucket, and the EC2 instance invokes both Amazon Bedrock and AWS Lambda using least-privilege IAM roles, without exposing credentials on disk.

Benefits and impact

A researcher, a fire safety engineer, or a habitat designer can answer within minutes what has been measured under certain conditions, with which source, and what remains unmeasured. This matters because upcoming missions will operate with atmospheres never tested before—for example, the proposed exploration atmosphere (0.57 atm, 34% O₂) falls outside everything measured by FLEX—. The coverage gap map itself guides where it makes sense to invest in the next experiments.

Limitations

The simulator is a demonstration model, not fully realistic; the 3D visualization is qualitative, meaning the findings are correlations across trials—coincidences in the data, not cause-and-effect relationships—. The conversational model is not infallible; it could fail, with a low probability, to retrieve all related references. Not all information contained in the datasets was indexed, meaning only text without video and images.
